author.name: AI News & Strategy Daily | Nate B Jones

media:group.media:title: Everyone's watching the wrong AI scoreboard #AI #OpenAI #AInews #tech #bigtech
media:group.media:description:
For two years, one number ran the entire AI industry: who has the best model this month. Every launch, every earnings call, every leak got scored against it, and that scoreboard justified the biggest capital buildout in the history of technology. It was not irrational. The model race was real and it produced real jumps.
But the tell is what the leaders are doing now. When the companies at the front quietly stop competing on the thing everyone else is still measuring, the game has already moved. The best model stops being the prize, and the fight shifts to who owns the context, the distribution, and the permission to ship. If you are still keeping score the old way, you are going to watch the wrong companies win and never quite understand why.
Here's the new race the leaders are actually running: https://natesnewsletter.substack.com/p/ai-race-context?r=1z4sm5&utm_campaign=post&utm_medium=web&showWelcomeOnShare=true

entry.title: Why does everything look the same now? #AI #creativity #marketing #futureofwork #AItools

author.name: AI News & Strategy Daily | Nate B Jones

media:group.media:title: Why does everything look the same now? #AI #creativity #marketing #futureofwork #AItools
media:group.media:description:
You have probably felt this without putting words to it. Everything coming out of AI is competent and clean and completely forgettable, and it all rhymes. Your post, the post right under it, the thing your competitor shipped, they could swap bylines and no one would notice. The reflex is to blame the tool, so people go shopping for a better model, and the sameness follows them there too.
Here is what actually happened. AI drove the cost of producing things to almost nothing, and the moment execution gets that cheap, execution stops being where the value lives. It does not vanish. It moves. It moves to the parts a model cannot hand you: taste, a real point of view, and knowing which thing is even worth making in the first place. If your work still competes on producing the artifact, you are competing in the one spot that just got commoditized.
More on where the value actually went: https://natesnewsletter.substack.com/p/beyond-model-routing?r=1z4sm5&utm_campaign=post&utm_medium=web&showWelcomeOnShare=true

entry.title: What if AI isn't the problem anymore? #AI #productivity #AItransformation #futureofwork #aitools

author.name: AI News & Strategy Daily | Nate B Jones

media:group.media:title: What if AI isn't the problem anymore? #AI #productivity #AItransformation #futureofwork #aitools
media:group.media:description:
Most people bought AI and then pointed it at the exact same to-do list they had two years ago. The emails still get written, just faster. The decks still get built, just cheaper. It feels like progress, and the tools genuinely are better, so it is easy to call that a transformation.
But look closely and nothing actually changed except the speed. Same tasks, same outputs, same shape of the work. When execution gets this cheap, doing your old list faster is the least interesting thing you can do with it. The people pulling ahead are not running the old list quicker. They are asking for things that were not even on the table a year ago, work they never would have attempted because it used to be too expensive or too slow.
That gap is not a tools gap. It is an imagination gap. Here's how to find the work actually worth pointing AI at: https://natesnewsletter.substack.com/p/beyond-model-routing?r=1z4sm5&utm_campaign=post&utm_medium=web&showWelcomeOnShare=true

Everyone's first objection to AI agents is the same, and it is a fair one. They hallucinate. You cannot trust them. So you end up hovering over every step, checking the work, and at that point you may as well have done it yourself.
Here is the thing that changes the math. The fix for an agent you cannot trust is not a smarter single agent. It is a second agent whose only job is to check the first one, and a third that checks that. When one of mine made something up, another one caught it and corrected it before it ever reached me. No hovering, no cleanup, no lifting a finger. The system polices itself, which is the only version of this that actually saves you time instead of handing you a babysitting job.

media:group.media:title: Stop building AI agents that just click buttons #AI #aiagents #automation #productivity #AItools
media:group.media:description:
Most agent demos show you the wrong magic trick. Watch, it clicked send. Watch, it booked the meeting. That is the easy part. You could always click send. What actually eats your week is everything that happens before the click: digging through a messy folder, making sense of a denial letter, pulling the right numbers out of a pile of unstructured junk that was never meant to be read quickly.
That is the part worth automating. An agent earns its place when it takes the bureaucratic mess and turns it into something clean enough that the final action is trivial. It does the reading, the sorting, the assembling. You stay in the seat for the one decision that actually carries risk, and you click the button yourself.
I built exactly this for insurance denials and tax piles, an agent that assembles the whole cited packet and then stops so you can review and send: https://natesnewsletter.substack.com/p/reusable-ai-agent?r=1z4sm5&utm_campaign=post&utm_medium=web&showWelcomeOnShare=true

media:group.media:title: The real thing gating AI now isn't the technology #OpenAI #AI #AIregulation #AInews #tech
media:group.media:description:
For two years the whole AI race was about one thing: who has the most compute and the best model. That story is quietly ending. The labs at the frontier are bumping into a different wall now, and it is not a technical one. It is political. When a government can decide whether and when your flagship model is allowed to ship, raw capability stops being the thing that wins, and access to permission becomes the real asset.
That is what the OpenAI government move is actually about. It is not goodwill and it is not safety theater. It is a company paying for regulatory headroom the same way it pays for data centers, because getting the model out the door is now a political problem as much as an engineering one. Once you see the race this way, a lot of the recent moves stop looking random.
The old "who has the best model" scoreboard is over. Here's the race that replaced it: https://natesnewsletter.substack.com/p/ai-race-context?r=1z4sm5&utm_campaign=post&utm_medium=web&showWelcomeOnShare=true

media:group.media:description:
For twenty years, size was the signal. A bigger agency meant more capacity, more safety, more reasons to trust them with the work. That signal is breaking. When a handful of people with good tools can turn around the same volume of work, the client starts doing math they never used to do, and the big team's headcount stops looking like strength and starts looking like the reason the invoice is so high.
The small shop will not win on reputation, and it does not need to. It wins on being faster, cheaper, and close enough on quality that the gap no longer justifies the premium. If you run a lean team, this is the biggest edge you have had in a generation. If you run the big one, the ground is moving under you.
I broke down exactly which firms AI protects and which ones it quietly guts here: https://natesnewsletter.substack.com/p/executive-briefing-the-bifurcated?r=1z4sm5&utm_campaign=post&utm_medium=web&showWelcomeOnShare=true
